 That the above observation, if analysed properly and correctly, itself indicates that the plaintiff has an arguable case to go for trial His further contention is that in the averments made by the plaintiff-appellant in the plaint as well as in the application for temporary injunction manifestly show that the plaintiff-society's registration dated 6.8.90 was valid for 2 years i.e. up to 5.8.92 and the plaintiff-appellant society was rightly allowed to take part in the bidding in the auction for the suit fisheries by filing tenders by the Nikly Upazila Nirbahi Officer, vide his Office Memo No.179(200) dated 9.3.92 and there was no cancellation of the said registration of the plaintiff-society as alleged and no such ground was also assigned in the bid-sheet while cancelling the tenders of the plaintiff-society but admittedly the plaintiff-society had taken part in the bidding and offered the highest tenders in case of auction of both the suit fisheries. He has further contended that it is the case of the plaintiff society that the defendant No. 1, the Chairman of the Tender Committee, being absent on 22.3.92 when the tender box was opened after 01-00 PM and the tenders were examined, it was unofficially disclosed that the plaintiff appellant society was the biggest tenderer for both the suit-fisheries and accordingly, the secretary of the plaintiff-appellant society left the spot for collection of the 50% bid money to be deposited at the time of formal and official declaration of the result of the bidding in question by the Tender Committee. By the above submission, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-appellant- society has tried to show that it had a legal right or claim to have the settlement of the suit fisheries in its favour and the cancellation of its highest tender was wholly illegal, malafide, arbitrary and void and not binding upon the plaintiff-appellant society and in that view of the matter it has a good prime facie arguable case for injunction. The learned Advocate for the plaintiff-appellant of course concedes that success of its above claim depends mainly on the consideration of the evidence that will be led at the trial of the suit. The learned Advocates appearing for the contesting defendant-respondent-opposite parties have however contended that according to the Rules of the Government Estate Manual, particularly rule 206, Government has the sole right to lease out the fisheries according to its discretion and it is not bound to accept the highest tender or bid and the same may be cancelled even without assigning any reason and in the instant case, the plaintiff-appellant-society was found to be incompetent to take part in the bidding as its registration was cancelled earlier and hence the plaintiff appellant society has no legal right or possession in the suit fisheries and therefore the learned Subordinate Judge has rightly observed that the plaintiff society has not been able to show any prime facie arguable case for temporary injunction. It is well settled that in case of the prayer for temporary injunction, it is the primary requirement for the plaintiff to show that he has good prime facie arguable case for injunction. Of course apart from that, in order to obtain an order of temporary injunction there are other two important requirements, namely, the balance of convenience and inconvenience and the question of irreparable loss that may be sustained by the plaintiff in case of non-granting of temporary injunction. The, above principles governing temporary injunctions have been well-settled in the case of Uttara Bank vs. Macneill and Kilburn Ltd. and others reported in 33 DLR (AD) 298, wherein it has been observed as follows:

We are in respectful agreement with the above observation and we must hold that mere showing of a prima facie case alone will not entitle the plaintiff-society to obtain an order or temporary injunction, unless the other two minimum requirements are satisfied. It may however be noticed in connection with the Rule arising out of the present First Misc. Appeal that 3 counter-affidavits have been separately filed by the 3 contesting defendant-respondent-opposite parties. One on behalf of the defendant-respondent-opposite party No. 9 and another on behalf of the defendant-respondent-opposite party No. 11 and the third one on behalf of the defendant respondent-opposite party No. 1 representing the Government. From these counter-affidavits along with some annexures, we find that the defendant-respondent-opposite party No. 1 has come to say that the registration of the plaintiff- society was cancelled by the Registrar, Co-operative Societies of Bangladesh by an order dated 20.8.91, as such, plaintiff society was incompetent to take part in any bidding of Government fisheries and the counter affidavit along with the annexures filed on behalf of the defendant-respondent-opposite party No.9 also shows that after payment of the entire bid-money for granting the lease of the first suit fishery in favour of the defendant-opposite party No.9, actual physical possession thereof has been delivered to the said society respondent-opposite party No.I9 and also a deed of lease for the said fishery has been executed by the Government in favour of the said defendant opposite party No.9 as required under the rules and so far the counter affidavit of the defendant-respondent-opposite party No.11 and the papers submitted' on its behalf, it appears that on acceptance of the full amount of the bid money the lease of the fishery as described in the second schedule of the plaint has been granted in its favour and the defendant No. 11 society has accordingly been put into physical possession of the said suit-fishery on 7.6.92 as described above. Of course there is no paper submitted before us as to the execution of the required lease-deed in favour of this society defendant No.11. Now, to determine the question of balance of convenience and inconvenience we may take into consideration the above facts and the documents appearing in the counter affidavits of the defendant-opposite parties which show that the defendant-societies 9 and 11 have already gone into possession of the suit-fisheries and the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for the defendant Respondent-Opposite party No.1 representing the Government has filed a counter-affidavit and admits the above position regarding lease of the suit fisheries and the possession of the Respondent opposite parties 9 and 11 over the same. It has been contended on behalf of all the contesting defendants-respondents-opposite parties by their respective Advocates that the balance of convenience and inconvenience is well in their favour and it was or is never in favour of the plaintiff-appellant society which will never sustain any irreparable loss. Now, Mr. Kaiser Uddin Ahmed, the learned Deputy Attorney-General while arguing on behalf of the Government has further raised the question of maintainability of the suit as well as the application for temporary injunction in view of sub-section (2) of section 76 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act which runs as follows: 

 11. Apparently, it appears that the provision relates to settlement of land vested in the Government, but it has to be examined whether it is applicable to the cases of settlement of fisheries also. Therefore at this stage we do not deem it proper and safe to give any finding as to the maintainability of the suit by way of reference to section 76 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Apart from that, in deciding the matter of temporary injunction upon an application under Order 39 rules 1 and 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure, maintainability of the suit should not be gone into and properly decided, particularly when there will be necessity of evidence at the trial of the suit for correctly deciding such issue. The present suit is not a suit of such a nature where without any evidence it can be correctly decided, at this stage that the suit is barred by any law.
